row.note: The commentary makes patience the act of holding one's own self; the proverb ranks the person who rules his spirit above a conqueror, turning restraint into strength.

The commentary contrasts self-restraint with being held by another; this proverb pictures a person without control of spirit as a city without walls, exposed precisely because the inner guard is absent.
The commentary defines patience as keeping the self from outcry; the psalmist says he has calmed and quieted his soul like a weaned child, giving that inner action a concrete image.
The commentary's patient person holds the self back from lament; the psalmist resolves to muzzle his mouth while the wicked stand before him, an intentional restraint of speech.
The commentary places the holding hand alongside restraint of the person; Job recalls princes stopping their words and putting a hand over their mouth, a visible enactment of self-control.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's asr includes restraining; Eliphaz asks who can restrain words when provoked, using Hebrew עצר for the failure of verbal self-control.

The commentary's passive captive is held for killing, while its patient person withholds an outcry; the servant is led like a lamb to slaughter and does not open his mouth, joining both positions in one scene.
The commentary contrasts being held by others with holding oneself; Jesus, under abuse, neither retaliates nor threatens but entrusts judgment to God, giving the captive person's restraint agency.

row.basis: captivity and the endurance of saints
row.note: The commentary opposes the person held by others to the one who practices patience; this verse names captivity and sword death, then identifies the saints' endurance and faith in that situation.
The commentary's prisoner is held toward death and the believer is urged to endure; the church is warned of imprisonment and called to remain faithful even to death.

The commentary calls fasting one form of holding the self and also depicts a person held against his will; Isaiah calls for a fast that loosens bonds and frees the oppressed, joining the two types of holding ethically.
The commentary juxtaposes fasting as restraint and the hand that withholds what it could give; Isaiah's chosen fast requires sharing bread with the hungry and bringing the homeless in.

row.basis: closing the hand to the poor
row.note: The commentary's tight-handed asir keeps back what he can give; the law forbids hardening the heart or closing the hand against a poor brother.
The commentary depicts the person who holds his hand against giving; this verse commands opening the hand and lending enough for the poor person's need.
The commentary calls the withholding hand a form of asr; the proverb forbids keeping good from those to whom it is due when one's hand has power to do it.
The commentary links the tight hand to the human being in loss; this proverb says one person withholds what ought to be given and comes to want, giving that loss an economic form.
The commentary's asir has the means to give but holds them; the letter asks how God's love remains in a person who sees a needy brother yet closes compassion while possessing worldly goods.

row.basis: failure to feed and give drink
row.note: The commentary treats the withholding hand as a moral failure; the condemned are told they gave no food or drink to the hungry and thirsty, making a withheld gift decisive in judgment.

row.basis: wealth holder begs relief from flame
row.note: The commentary places withholding beside daring toward fire; the rich man who ignored Lazarus now begs for a finger dipped in water to cool him in the flame, reversing who needs the other's hand.
The commentary's gain-hoarding person becomes the one held to loss; Abraham tells the rich man that Lazarus now receives comfort while he is in anguish, explaining the reversal after their lifetimes.

The commentary pairs a bad purchase with loss and fire; Jesus asks what profit there is in gaining the whole world while forfeiting one's life, a pointed counterpart to buying error at the cost of guidance.

The commentary's inverted patience is brazen acceptance of fire after a bad bargain; Daniel's companions refuse the idol even without rescue, making courage before threatened fire serve fidelity instead.
The commentary's wrongdoers are daring toward punitive fire; in Daniel the king sees the faithful captives walking unharmed in the furnace, reversing the moral reason for facing fire and its outcome.
The commentary includes the hand that withholds available goods; Lazarus longs for the crumbs from the rich man's table, so the later flame follows a specific unshared surplus.

The commentary's phrase about daring toward fire exposes the folly of accepting destructive consequences; the proverb asks whether one can carry fire against the chest without burning one's clothes, in its context a warning against adultery.

The commentary links a ruinous choice to apparent boldness before fire; those who kindle their own fire are told to walk by its flames and will lie down in torment, making the chosen flame a judgment.
The commentary places a withholding hand beside fire as a dire end; the judgment scene sends those on the left to eternal fire, with their failure to feed and welcome specified in the next verse.

row.basis: king imposes oath and food restraint
row.note: The commentary distinguishes chosen fasting from a man forcibly made to swear; Saul binds his troops with an oath not to eat until evening, turning restraint into an imposed burden.

row.basis: fear of oath keeps hands from food
row.note: The commentary depicts forced oath and a restrained hand; Saul's troops see honey but no one puts a hand to his mouth because they fear the oath, showing bodily cost of imposed restraint.
The commentary's captive is made to swear and faces death; the high priest adjures the previously silent Jesus by the living God to answer about his identity during the trial.
The commentary names a father holding back his son's property; the angel says Abraham has not withheld his son from God, reversing the direction and object of a father's withholding.

row.basis: limit on father's disposal of inheritance
row.note: The commentary pictures a father holding back what belongs to a son; the law bars a father from favoring a later son with the firstborn's portion, constraining paternal control of property.

row.basis: father divides property at son's request
row.note: The commentary's father withholds a child's goods; the younger son requests his share and the father divides the estate, a narrative reversal of paternal withholding.

row.basis: father says all his goods are son's
row.note: The commentary raises the possibility of a father retaining a son's property; the father assures the elder son that everything he has is his, distinguishing possession from a closed paternal hand.
The commentary's newly menstruating girl is kept at home; this law situates a young woman's vow while she remains in her father's house, where his authority can affect her commitment.
The commentary's held girl is subject to a household's control; the father can forbid the vow he hears and the daughter is released from it, a concrete form of paternal restraint in that house.

row.basis: father's authority over minor daughter's goods and vows
row.note: The commentary joins a father controlling a child's property with a young girl kept at home; this legal tradition enumerates a father's rights over his minor daughter's betrothal, earnings, finds and vows, clarifying how household custody includes economic control.

row.basis: Mary removed from temple at puberty
row.note: The commentary calls the newly menstruating girl one kept in the house; the priests seek a guardian for twelve-year-old Mary lest her approaching maturity defile the sanctuary, an early Christian account of seclusion and relocation around puberty.
The commentary extends self-restraint from a person to a community; Joel orders a sanctified fast and calls a solemn assembly, using the table's Hebrew עצר family for the collective gathering.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's asr includes holding back; the seventh day is an עצרת, a restrained festival assembly in which no work is done, joining communal gathering to a prohibition on action.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's passive patient is confined by others; the Assyrian king confines Hoshea and binds him in prison, using Hebrew עצר for involuntary custody.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary pairs being held with a divine word received while waiting; Jeremiah is still confined in the court of the guard when the Lord's word comes to him, using עצר for custody.

row.basis: Lord's eye on those who wait
row.note: The commentary tells the waiting prophet that he is under God's eyes; this psalm says the Lord's eye rests on those who fear him and wait for his faithful love, joining watchfulness to expectation.
The commentary's patient servant waits under divine sight; the seer says the Lord's eyes range through the earth to strengthen those fully loyal to him, making observation a source of support.

row.basis: God's eyes and ears attend the righteous
row.note: The commentary says the waiting person is under God's eyes; this letter applies the scriptural formula of the Lord's eyes toward the righteous and ears toward their prayer, giving the watched person a hearing as well.
The commentary invokes the fish's owner as the example a patient prophet must avoid; the Hebrew story first has a great fish swallow Jonah, making his literal confinement the setting of that warning.
The commentary recalls the fish's owner crying out while constrained; in Hebrew verse numbering Jonah prays to the Lord from the fish's belly, turning confinement into an appeal.
The commentary warns the waiting prophet not to be like the constricted fish's owner; later Jonah tells God he is angry enough to die, identifying the uncontrolled reaction at issue.
The commentary defines patience as waiting under God's judgment without outcry; Lamentations calls it good to wait quietly for the Lord's salvation amid suffering.

row.basis: sitting alone in silence under imposed burden
row.note: The commentary distinguishes holding oneself from being held by another; the sufferer is told to sit alone and silent because a yoke has been laid on him, holding both experiences together.
The commentary's patience includes waiting rather than merely suppression; James asks believers to be patient until the Lord's coming like a farmer awaiting the crop and its rains.
The commentary tells the prophet to wait for the Lord's judgment; Hebrews says believers need endurance to do God's will and receive what was promised, connecting delay with obedient action.

row.basis: God limits trial and makes endurance possible
row.note: The commentary joins patient endurance to being under divine care; Paul says God will not allow a trial beyond capacity and will provide a way to endure it.
The commentary makes patience something believers commend to each other; Hebrews commands daily mutual exhortation lest any heart be hardened by sin.

row.basis: spur one another to love and good works
row.note: The commentary's mutual counsel sits beside faith and righteous action; Hebrews asks members to consider how to provoke one another toward love and good deeds.

row.basis: mutual encouragement as the day approaches
row.note: The commentary expands restraint to a persevering group; Hebrews warns against abandoning assembly and calls for encouraging one another as the day draws near.

row.basis: warn, encourage, support, be patient with all
row.note: The commentary's patience is a shared duty rather than an isolated virtue; Paul orders the community to admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak and be patient toward all.

row.basis: bear with and forgive one another
row.note: The commentary calls believers to recommend patience to one another; Colossians makes that reciprocal by asking each person to bear with and forgive another after a complaint.
The commentary extends the held self to a community that holds together; Ephesians names patience and bearing with one another in love as conduct worthy of the calling.
The commentary groups faith, good action and mutual patience as the exception to loss; Revelation identifies the saints' endurance with keeping God's commandments and faith in Jesus.
The commentary puts faith beside patience in the saved community; Hebrews tells readers to imitate those who inherit promises through faith and patience.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
row.note: The commentary's insan is vulnerable to loss yet addressed by divine care; the psalm asks why God remembers mortal enosh, setting human frailty beside God's attention.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
row.note: The commentary's insan is one held under divine judgment; Job asks why God makes so much of mortal enosh and sets his heart on him, casting close attention as oppressive in his suffering.
The commentary says the patient waits under God's eyes as protection; Job complains that God visits and tests him every morning, preserving a contrary experience of divine surveillance.

row.basis: ء ن س / Aramaic אנש, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's insan is mortal and at risk of loss; Daniel sees a figure like a son of enash coming with the clouds toward the Ancient of Days, giving the human designation a strikingly exalted setting.

row.basis: kingdom granted to the humanlike figure
row.note: The commentary describes humanity in loss and then an exception; the figure introduced as a son of enash in the previous verse receives an enduring dominion here, making the reversal explicit.

row.basis: kingdom given to oppressed holy people
row.note: The commentary makes believing endurance the exception to human loss; after the preceding vision of oppression, Daniel gives the kingdom to the people of the holy ones, a corporate reversal of defeat.

row.basis: fear of dying mortal against divine comfort
row.note: The commentary calls the human being frail and liable to loss; God asks why the comforted people fear mortal enosh who dies like grass, while divine reassurance remains available.

row.basis: mortal man heaps wealth without knowing heir
row.note: The commentary's tight hand is set beside humanity's loss; this psalm says a person heaps wealth without knowing who will gather it, using צבר, the table's sound match to ص ب ر, here meaning accumulation rather than patience.

row.basis: wait for God after futile hoarding
row.note: The commentary opposes possessive holding to patient waiting; immediately after describing a person heaping goods without knowing their heir, the psalmist asks what he waits for and names God as hope.

The commentary's withholding hand accumulates goods under threat of loss; Job says the wicked may heap up silver like dust, using צבר, the table's sound match to ص ب ر with the distinct sense of accumulation.

row.basis: stored goods pass to the innocent
row.note: The commentary's human holder cannot keep his gain secure; Job says the innocent will divide the wicked person's silver, reversing the hoard described in the preceding verse.

row.basis: Tyre heaps wealth behind a fortress
row.note: The commentary associates protected stores with a potentially grasping hand; Tyre builds a stronghold and heaps silver and gold like dust, using צבר, the table's sound match to ص ب ر with the distinct sense of piling up.

row.basis: stored wealth lost and city consumed by fire
row.note: The commentary links hoarding with ultimate fire; after Tyre's fortified accumulation, the Lord strips its wealth and fire consumes it, showing how a guarded store fails.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's asr can enclose a girl at reproductive maturity; Sarai says the Lord has restrained her from bearing children, using עצר for an involuntary bodily restriction rather than household confinement.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's house-held girl connects enclosure with reproduction; God has closed the wombs throughout Abimelech's household because of Sarah, using עצר for reproductive restraint, a different subject and cause.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's collective patience joins moral action to communal holding; God rejects an עצרה, a solemn assembly, when worship is mixed with injustice, warning that the gathered form alone does not suffice.
The commentary allows holding to describe a whole community; the eighth-day sacred assembly, called עצרת from the table's Hebrew עצר family, is paired with a ban on ordinary work.

row.basis: grain is crushed but not endlessly
row.note: The commentary's grain is protected in its covering; Isaiah distinguishes grain processing from destruction, saying it is threshed but not pulverized forever, an agricultural counterpart to protection before use.
The commentary imagines grain sheltered in its covering; the winnower separates wheat from chaff and gathers the grain into storage, showing the covering removed when preservation takes a new form.
The commentary's enclosed grain is kept for safety; Joseph proposes keeping grain as a reserve for famine so the land will not perish, shifting protection from a husk to a storehouse.
The commentary's grain is something held in reserve; Joseph stores so much grain that it becomes uncountable, a beneficial form of withholding set against the commentary's selfish tight hand.

The commentary's grain remains protected in its covering; Jesus says a grain that does not fall into the earth and die remains alone, while dying makes it fruitful, a contrary claim about when protected seed must be released.

The commentary makes fasting a kind of self-restraint yet warns about holding others; Isaiah rebukes fasters who pursue their own business and oppress workers on the fast day, exposing the split between the two acts.

row.basis: communal fast judged by changed deeds
row.note: The commentary broadens patience to a community and calls fasting a form of restraint; this fast-day exhortation says the people of Nineveh were heeded for changed deeds, making a gathered fast accountable to conduct.
The commentary treats fasting as an inward holding of the self; Jesus warns fasters against disfiguring their faces to be seen by others, distinguishing the act from theatrical self-display.

The commentary connects patience with waiting and fasting with self-restraint; Jesus says the wedding guests will fast when the bridegroom is taken away, giving voluntary abstinence the time of an absence.
The commentary extends patient holding from a person to a group; the Antioch church worships and fasts when the Spirit speaks, placing shared restraint beside guidance and action.
The commentary makes fasting one form of patience in a community; the Didache prescribes shared weekly fast days, showing how the act became a repeated group discipline.
The commentary defines patience as holding the self rather than being held; the saying calls one who conquers his own inclination mighty, interpreting power as inward mastery.

The commentary's holding hand can be stingy; the Didache asks that alms remain in the hand until the giver knows the recipient, a distinct form of temporary restraint meant to guide giving rather than avoid it.

The commentary's asir withholds resources; this church exhortation tells the rich to supply the poor person's need and the poor to thank God for the provider, turning possession into a reciprocal relation.
The commentary sets forced oath beside the tight hand; Paul tells each person to give as decided in the heart, not under compulsion, so the release of goods is neither hoarding nor coercion.

row.basis: good wishes without food or clothing
row.note: The commentary makes withheld goods a failure of the hand; James asks what good it does to wish warmth and fullness to a needy person without providing bodily necessities.
The commentary's asir is marked by a hand held closed; the righteous person in this proverb gives and does not hold back, after the preceding clause describes craving all day.
The commentary names a father withholding a son's goods; the proverb praises a good person who leaves an inheritance to grandchildren, a long view of wealth passed on rather than retained.

row.basis: father asked for bread does not give stone
row.note: The commentary imagines a father's hand controlling what his child receives; Jesus' question assumes a father responds to a son's request for bread with food rather than a useless stone.
The commentary includes grain kept in protection and wealth held back; the rich farmer plans larger barns for his grain and goods, joining storage to the closed-hand danger.
The commentary's possessor is still a mortal held to account; God demands the rich farmer's life that night and asks who will own the stored goods, overturning the fantasy of secure possession.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנס, table sound match; compulsion, not human cognate
row.note: The commentary's forced oath shows one person restraining another; Esther's banquet rule says drinking is without compulsion, a specific reversal of social coercion, though the act is drinking rather than swearing and the Hebrew root is not used for a human being.
The commentary mentions a man made to swear by another; Solomon's prayer envisages an oath being laid on an accused man at the altar and asks God to judge, giving imposed swearing a judicial setting.

row.basis: truthful speech in place of oaths
row.note: The commentary's oath scene makes another person control a man's speech; James forbids oath-taking and asks for plain yes and no, a response to the moral vulnerability of sworn speech.

row.basis: confined speaker sends his words outward
row.note: The commentary contrasts a held person with mutually recommended truth; Jeremiah says he is detained and cannot enter the Lord's house, then instructs Baruch to read his scroll there, showing testimony moving despite confinement.

row.basis: prisoners pray and sing while bound
row.note: The commentary's captive can still practice an active form of patience; Paul and Silas pray and sing hymns at midnight in prison while other prisoners listen.

row.basis: be still while waiting for the Lord
row.note: The commentary says waiting is a form of patience under divine judgment; the psalm orders the hearer to be still before the Lord and wait rather than fret over a prospering schemer.
The commentary's prophet is told to endure while awaiting the Lord's decision; James names the prophets who spoke in the Lord's name as examples of suffering and patience.
The commentary joins waiting under pain to divine care; James calls those who endured blessed and points to Job's endurance and the Lord's compassionate outcome.
The commentary defines patience as holding back lament under misfortune; Job rebukes his wife's counsel and accepts adversity from God without sinning with his lips in this scene.

row.basis: patient in affliction and constant in prayer
row.note: The commentary's waiting person restrains panic under God's eyes; Paul joins patience in suffering to persistence in prayer, making endurance an active appeal.
The commentary moves from one person's held self to shared endurance; Paul commands believers to bear one another's burdens, giving collective patience a practical action.

row.basis: whole household called out to assembly
row.note: The commentary expands holding to a community and evokes domestic enclosure; Joel summons elders, children, nursing infants and even bride and groom from their rooms, showing the fast superseding ordinary household boundaries.

row.basis: guardian decides about young woman's marriage
row.note: The commentary's girl is subject to household control at maturity; one reading of Paul's ambiguous reference to a man's virgin and her passing youth concerns a father's decision about marriage, though the passage can also be read of a betrothed couple.

row.basis: prisoners groan and are marked for death
row.note: The commentary's passive patient is someone held for killing; the psalm asks God to hear imprisoned people's groans and preserve those appointed to die, adding a plea for release to the captive scene.

The commentary's bad exchange is followed by daring toward fire; Ezekiel condemns unjust trading and says fire will come from the trader's midst and consume him, bringing commerce and punishment into one verse.
The commentary says a person can be held as security for what he has earned; the unforgiving servant imprisons a fellow debtor until he pays, making financial liability literal captivity.

row.basis: unforgiving creditor made the detained debtor
row.note: The commentary contrasts the hand that withholds with the one who becomes held; the master hands the unmerciful servant over to jailers until his debt is paid, reversing his role in the previous imprisonment.

The commentary links a father's control of goods to the person forcibly held; indebted families say their daughters are already enslaved and their fields belong to others, showing a household's loss of both property and freedom.

row.basis: impatient merchants wait out rest to sell grain
row.note: The commentary sets patient communal restraint against the grasping hand and protected grain; merchants ask when the new moon and sabbath will end so they can sell grain with dishonest measures, turning waiting into greed.

row.basis: buying the poor and selling inferior grain
row.note: The commentary's bad bargain and tight hand harm other people; Amos accuses merchants of buying the needy for silver and selling sweepings of wheat, joining unjust exchange to grain.
The commentary says humans cry out under harm yet withhold good when they have it; the proverb warns that one who shuts his ear to the poor person's cry will cry out and receive no answer.

row.basis: unjust gain takes the owner's life
row.note: The commentary's bargain for error leads to loss; the proverb says ill-gotten gain takes away the life of its possessors, making acquisition turn against the acquirer.

The commentary's father-and-son property scene raises goods held from rightful users; Nehemiah demands that lenders return debtors' fields and houses and remit the interest, providing a communal remedy for the grasping hand.
The commentary's captive is held toward death; Jesus' reading of Isaiah announces release to captives, supplying a counter movement to the image of enforced confinement.

row.basis: facing lethal torment for covenant hope
row.note: The commentary's inverted patience is rash boldness before fire after rejecting guidance; the tortured brother tells his killer that God will raise those who die for God's laws, a contrary reason for accepting death.

The commentary makes patience a virtue commended between people; the mother watches her seven sons die in one day and bears it with courage because of hope in the Lord, a family form of shared endurance.

The commentary distinguishes a person holding himself from another holding his hand, then extends patience to a group; Aaron and Hur physically support Moses' tired hands until sunset while the people endure battle.

row.basis: remember prisoners as bound with them
row.note: The commentary's person held by others remains part of the patient community; Hebrews tells readers to remember prisoners as though bound alongside them, turning shared endurance into solidarity.

row.basis: visit the one held in prison
row.note: The commentary places the captive beside the hand that may withhold good; the righteous are commended for coming to the speaker while he was in prison, an action addressed specifically to the held person.
The commentary's withholding hand and detained person meet in one moral scene; the condemned are told they did not visit the speaker when he was sick or in prison.

row.basis: wrongdoer held by cords of his sin
row.note: The commentary says each person is held to what he has earned; the proverb makes that relation physical when the wicked person's own iniquities ensnare him and the cords of his sin hold him fast.

row.basis: holy ones handed over for a limited time
row.note: The commentary speaks of an afflicted group that must endure together; Daniel's arrogant king wears out the holy ones and they are given into his hand for a stated time before the kingdom changes hands.
The commentary calls humanity lost except for those who practice patience; Jesus tells persecuted hearers that by their endurance they will gain their lives, linking loss and preservation directly.

row.basis: discipline body and make it a slave
row.note: The commentary sets holding oneself beside being held by another; Paul says he disciplines and enslaves his own body lest he be disqualified, deliberately combining the two positions in one person.
The commentary moves from a person's restraining hand to mutual encouragement; Isaiah commands hearers to strengthen weak hands, making the community's support of frail members concrete.

row.basis: say to the anxious to be strong
row.note: The commentary's believers recommend patience to one another under divine care; Isaiah tells them to address fearful hearts with courage and the promise that God will come and save.

The commentary's exception to loss includes mutual counsel in truth; Zechariah commands people to speak truth with their neighbors and render true judgments for peace, giving that counsel a public setting.

row.basis: truth spoken because members belong together
row.note: The commentary joins truth to reciprocal counsel within the group; Ephesians tells each person to speak truth to a neighbor because believers are members of one another.
The commentary says the saved community commends truth and patience to its members; Colossians commands mutual teaching and admonition with wisdom, turning shared conviction into speech.

row.basis: reprove neighbor instead of harboring wrong
row.note: The commentary's mutual counsel requires another person's good; the law commands frank correction of a neighbor rather than silently bearing sin on his account.

row.basis: oath threatens an unwitting eater with death
row.note: The commentary's forced oath and captive held for killing are separate senses of restraint; Saul's oath leads him to pronounce death on Jonathan for eating honey, showing how an imposed restraint can endanger a person.

row.basis: community rescues person condemned by oath
row.note: The commentary makes endurance and right action communal; Saul's people refuse to let Jonathan die under the oath and rescue him, countering imposed restraint through collective intervention.

row.basis: Shimei ordered to remain in one city
row.note: The commentary's passive patient is held by another's command; Solomon orders Shimei to build a house in Jerusalem and stay there, making domestic residence a form of custody.

row.basis: king recalls oath tied to confinement
row.note: The commentary names a man compelled to swear and then held under another's control; Solomon reminds Shimei of the oath attached to his Jerusalem confinement after he crossed its boundary.

row.basis: confinement and oath end in execution
row.note: The commentary's coerced oath can converge with being held for death; Solomon orders Shimei executed after finding he violated the oath governing his residence.

row.basis: oath-bound abstinence used to plan murder
row.note: The commentary calls fasting a type of self-restraint yet also depicts forced oath and a person held for death; conspirators bind themselves by an oath to eat and drink nothing until they kill Paul, turning restraint into violence.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound match; shut rain
row.note: The commentary's asr includes holding back, and its grain is protected from loss; God warns that he may shut the heavens so rain and produce cease, using the table's Hebrew עצר correspondence for a communal loss of harvest.

row.basis: ع ص ر / עצר, table sound correspondence
row.note: The commentary's held grain and waiting community depend on what is released; Solomon envisions heaven restrained from rain because of sin and asks that prayer and repentance be heard, using עצר for divine withholding.

row.basis: wait for the delayed appointed time
row.note: The commentary presents patience as waiting for the Lord's decision; Habakkuk says the vision has an appointed time and instructs the hearer to wait even if it delays.

The commentary joins belief to patience as the exception to loss; Habakkuk contrasts the proud person's disordered soul with the righteous one who lives by faithfulness in the delay described just before.

row.basis: one who trusts need not hurry
row.note: The commentary sets belief and patient restraint against the human being's haste; Isaiah says the person who trusts the tested foundation will not be hurried, joining trust to freedom from panic.

The commentary says salvation belongs to those who restrain themselves in faith; God tells Judah that quietness and trust would be their strength, then says they were unwilling, making refusal of patience explicit.

The commentary's hasty human will not hold himself; Judah chooses swift horses rather than quiet trust and is told that flight and pursuit will follow, a concrete outcome of the refusal in the previous verse.
The commentary opposes the human being's quick distress to holding the self; James commands everyone to be quick to hear but slow to speak and slow to anger.
The commentary's patience is the contrary of impulsive human outcry; the proverb contrasts a person slow to anger with one quick tempered who exalts folly.

row.basis: do not hasten to anger in spirit
row.note: The commentary makes patience the restraining of inner agitation; Ecclesiastes warns against being quick in spirit to anger because anger lodges with fools.

row.basis: stored goods mistaken for long rest
row.note: The commentary opposes prudent waiting to a hand that hoards; the rich farmer tells his soul to rest for many years on stored goods, an imagined secure future overturned by the divine demand in the next verse.

row.basis: Satan seeks to sift disciples like wheat
row.note: The commentary's grain is kept in its covering and the community must endure pressure; Jesus says Satan has demanded to sift the disciples like wheat, turning grain processing into an image of testing the group.

The commentary's waiting believer is under protective divine attention and encourages others; Jesus says he has prayed that Peter's faith not fail and tells him to strengthen his brothers after he turns back.

row.basis: naked grain sown without its mature covering
row.note: The commentary pictures grain guarded by a surrounding husk; Paul says what is sown is a bare grain rather than the body it will have, placing fruitfulness at the point where the old covering is relinquished.

row.basis: self-control and prayer near the end
row.note: The commentary links the passing time, the held self and an exception marked by prayer; Peter says the end is near and therefore calls believers to sound judgment and sobriety for prayer.

The commentary extends patience from one person to a mutually enduring community; Peter tells believers to resist firmly in faith, knowing the same sufferings are being completed among their brothers and sisters elsewhere.

row.basis: care for prisoners despite property loss
row.note: The commentary sets imprisoned people beside the hand that guards possessions; Hebrews recalls sympathy for prisoners and joyful acceptance of property being seized because the community knew of a better possession.
The commentary says waiting occurs under God's watch and ends in judgment; this verse interprets apparent divine delay as patience toward people, giving them time to repent rather than perish.

The commentary ties daring toward fire to a ruinous moral choice; after describing the world's fiery dissolution, Peter asks what holy and godly conduct is required, reversing reckless exposure into ethical preparation.
The commentary treats patience as a held response to wrongdoing; Paul says God's kindness, forbearance and patience are meant to lead the human being to repentance, extending restraint to God.
The commentary's person can hoard what becomes loss at judgment; Paul says a hard, unrepentant heart stores up wrath for the day of God's judgment, a negative counterpart to storing goods.

row.basis: divine patience toward those facing destruction
row.note: The commentary sets patient restraint beside judgment on the human being; Paul describes God enduring with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, delaying the punitive end.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
row.note: The commentary's insan is in loss except for right action; Eliphaz asks whether mortal enosh can be righteous before God, pressing the frail human term into a question about moral standing.

row.basis: ء ن س / אנש, table sound correspondence with BDB Arabic note
row.note: The commentary's insan stands inside passing time; the psalm compares the days of mortal enosh to grass and a field flower, making human duration visibly fragile.

row.basis: unjust gain used to build a safe nest
row.note: The commentary's withholding hand tries to protect what it has gathered; Habakkuk condemns one who gains evil profit for his house to place his nest high beyond disaster.

row.basis: hoarder's plan costs his own life
row.note: The commentary's possessor becomes the one in loss; Habakkuk says the plan to cut off many peoples has brought shame on the house and forfeited its maker's life, undoing the security sought in the prior verse.

row.basis: mouth put in dust while hope remains
row.note: The commentary describes patience as holding back the cry while awaiting deliverance; after the instruction to sit silently under a yoke, Lamentations bids the sufferer put his mouth in dust because hope may remain.

row.basis: prisoner asks release and righteous company
row.note: The commentary's held person needs both rescue and the community's patient support; in Hebrew verse numbering the psalmist asks to be brought out of confinement so he can praise God among the righteous.
The commentary moves from a restraining hand to mutually commended endurance; Jonathan comes to David in danger and strengthens his hand in God, turning the hand into an image of encouragement.
The commentary's passive patient is held by another; the servant's commission includes telling prisoners to come out and those in darkness to show themselves, reversing enforced enclosure.

row.basis: kept word of endurance, then guarded from trial
row.note: The commentary links mutual persistence with being kept under divine eyes; the risen speaker promises to keep a faithful community from the hour of trial because it has kept his word of endurance.
The commentary's patience means waiting for a divine outcome one cannot yet see; Paul says believers wait for what they do not see through endurance.
The commentary puts faith and patience together as the exception to human loss; James says the testing of faith produces steadfastness, explaining how the two qualities meet in affliction.
The commentary describes humanity as in loss unless patience joins faith and good action; James asks that steadfastness complete its work so the believer may be complete and lack nothing.

row.basis: endured the cross for a future joy
row.note: The commentary contrasts a captive facing death with voluntary patience; Jesus endures the cross and shame for the joy set before him, giving purpose to restraint under execution.

row.basis: athlete exercises self-control for a crown
row.note: The commentary calls fasting a bodily form of holding oneself; Paul says athletes exercise self-control in all things for a perishable crown, then points to an imperishable aim.
The commentary identifies fasting as one kind of patience; Jesus fasts forty days and nights and becomes hungry, presenting abstinence as bodily restraint with a cost.

The commentary places being restrained beside patient trust; Moses says God humbled Israel by hunger and fed it manna so it would learn to live by what comes from God's mouth, a communal education through withheld food.

row.basis: fasting savings given to needy people
row.note: The commentary places fasting beside the hand that can withhold goods; Hermas' instruction directs a faster to give the cost of the uneaten meal to someone in need, making bodily restraint release resources.

The commentary pairs fasting as self-restraint with the ethical problem of withholding; this rabbinic maxim makes charity the reward or fruit of a fast, interpreting abstinence through what the hand gives.

row.basis: give from possessions without turning away
row.note: The commentary's withholding hand closes before the needy; Tobit instructs his son to give alms from his possessions and not turn his face from the poor, joining family counsel to generosity.
The commentary moves from hoarded goods to a person held toward death; Tobit says almsgiving delivers from death and keeps one from darkness, assigning the opened hand a rescuing effect.

row.basis: withheld help makes needy eyes wait
row.note: The commentary places waiting beside a hand that withholds; Sirach forbids depriving the poor of life and making the needy person's eyes wait, showing how one person's grasping imposes another's patience.
The commentary defines patience as holding one's own self; Sirach tells the hearer not to follow desires but to restrain appetites, directing the holding inward.
The commentary asks the afflicted person to wait under God's judgment rather than cry out; Sirach tells the hearer to accept what befalls him and be patient in humiliation.

row.basis: torturers test a righteous person's forbearance
row.note: The commentary's captive held for killing and the patient person can be the same individual; the wicked propose tormenting the righteous man to test his gentleness and forbearance.

row.basis: righteous person condemned to shameful death
row.note: The commentary's passive patient is restrained toward death; the wicked resolve to condemn the tested righteous man to a shameful death while claiming God will protect him, making the test lethal.

The commentary treats patience as holding the self even under pressure; the work opens by arguing that pious reason governs passions, a Jewish interpretation of disciplined endurance developed in its martyr stories.

The commentary's newly menstruating girl is held inside a house; the law assigns seven days of menstrual impurity and limits contact, supplying a ritual background for seclusion without itself ordering house confinement.

The commentary places a girl under a father's control and also describes forced oath; Jephthah tells his daughter he has vowed to the Lord and cannot take it back, so his own oath determines her fate, though she did not swear it.

row.basis: part of sale proceeds held back secretly
row.note: The commentary's holding hand can turn into deception; Ananias keeps part of the proceeds while presenting a gift as though complete, so the retained amount is tied to false speech.

row.basis: property remained at the giver's disposal
row.note: The commentary's tight hand is blameworthy when it refuses a rightful good; Peter says the field and its price remained under Ananias's authority, specifying that his wrongdoing was deceit rather than mere retention.

row.basis: harmful designs and false oaths rejected
row.note: The commentary's communal truth-telling stands beside a coerced oath; Zechariah forbids plotting evil against a neighbor and loving a false oath, guarding the group against speech used to injure.
The commentary makes patience something believers counsel each other to practice; Paul directly tells the community to encourage one another and build each other up.

row.basis: plain yes and no rather than sworn control
row.note: The commentary's man is made to swear by someone else; Jesus directs hearers toward plain yes and no, supplying a form of truthful speech that does not depend on an imposed oath.

The commentary juxtaposes enforced custody with endurance; Paul lists imprisonments alongside hard work, sleeplessness and hunger among apostolic hardships, preceding the patience named in the next verse.

The commentary's patient community has to answer distress with good action; Paul follows the preceding list of prisons and deprivations by naming patience and kindness among the qualities of his ministry.
The commentary's fast is a kind of self-restraint oriented toward divine judgment; when hungry after fasting, Jesus answers temptation by saying human life depends on God's word as well as bread.

The commentary sets patient holding beside grasping gain; the proverb says wealth gained hastily shrinks while one who gathers little by little increases it, assigning different outcomes to two tempos of acquisition.

The commentary links the human hand's surplus to later loss; the rich man dresses luxuriously and feasts every day while Lazarus lies at his gate in the next verse, establishing what could have been shared.
